title: TOXOPLASMOSIS: THE FOCAL RETINITIS MASTERCLASS
summary: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan and the most common identifiable cause of focal retinitis worldwide. This comprehensive guide covers the lifecycle, clinical manifestations, and the 'classic' vs. modern management protocols for ocular toxoplasmosis.

sections.title: The Pathogen & Global Burden
content: Causative Agent: Toxoplasma gondii (obligate intracellular protozoan).
Northern Temperate Countries: Estimated 10% adult infestation.
Mediterranean & Tropical Countries: Over 50% adult infestation.
Brazil: Responsible for up to 85% of posterior uveitis cases.
Global Posterior Uveitis: Accounts for 20–60% of all cases.
Primary Ocular Presentation: Average age of 29 years (likely due to decreasing immunity).

branches: Definitive Host: Cats (Oocysts excreted in faeces)
Intermediate Hosts: Humans, livestock, birds, rodents
Inactive Stage: Bradyzoite (Dormant in tissue cysts: eye, brain, skeletal muscle)
Active Form: Tachyzoite (Proliferating form released upon cyst rupture)
Transmission: Ingestion of contaminated water/soil, cat litter disposal, undercooked meat/eggs
Medical Transmission: Organ transplantation, Blood transfusion, Transplacental spread

rows: Congenital
Often subclinical; 10% result in fetal death. 75%+ have retinochoroiditis. Severity depends on gestation duration (worse in early pregnancy).
Postnatal Childhood
Accounts for >50% of childhood cases. Usually subclinical. Ocular lesions may develop years later.
Immunocompetent Adults
80–90% subclinical. Symptomatic: Cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, pharyngitis. Retinitis in up to 20%.
Immunocompromised
Reactivation or acquired. Risks: Meningoencephalitis, pneumonitis, fulminant retinochoroiditis.

sections.title: Ocular Presentation & Symptoms
content: Symptoms: Unilateral acute/subacute floaters, blurring, and photophobia.
Spill-over Anterior Uveitis: Common; can be granulomatous or resemble FUS. Elevated IOP may occur.
Typical Lesion: Fluffy white retinitis associated with a pigmented 'satellite' scar.
Vitritis: Often severe. 'Headlight in the fog' appearance (inflammatory nidus viewed through vitreous haze).
Vasculitis: More commonly venous than arterial.
Optic Disc: Oedema is common.
Punctate Outer Retinal Toxoplasmosis: Small (25–75 μm) grey-white lesions in younger patients.
Neuroretinitis: Rare; marker of acutely acquired infection (mimics cat-scratch).

rows: Viral Retinitis (ARN/PORN)
More rapid progression, peripheral location, lack of adjacent pigmented scars (usually).
Syphilis
Can mimic any uveitis; 'ground glass' vitritis, positive treponemal serology.
Cat-Scratch (Bartonella)
Neuroretinitis with macular star; history of cat scratch/bite; negative Toxo serology.
Sarcoidosis/TB
Granulomatous uveitis, but usually lacks the focal necrotizing retinitis and satellite scar.
Candidiasis
Multifocal 'fluff-balls' in vitreous; history of IV access/candidemia.

sections.title: Complications Leading to Vision Loss
content: Overall Risk: Permanent vision reduction in 25% of eyes.
Macular Pathology: Inflammatory lesions, oedema, and late secondary neovascularization.
Vascular: Retinal vascular occlusion (periarteritis).
Structural: Serous, rhegmatogenous, or tractional retinal detachment.
Optic Nerve: Involvement leading to atrophy.
Healing: Spontaneous resolution in 6–8 weeks (immunocompetent); vitreous takes longer.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: 1. Clinical Exam: Primary method of diagnosis.
2. Serology (IgG): Indicates past exposure; 1/3 community seroprevalence.
3. Serology (IgM): Indicates infection within 1 year; critical in pregnancy.
4. Goldmann–Witmer Coefficient: Ratio of specific IgG in aqueous vs. serum (48–90% sensitivity).
5. PCR Testing: Intraocular fluid; highly specific, variable sensitivity (16–67%).
6. Imaging (OCT/B-Scan): Monitor macular oedema or exclude RD in severe vitritis.
7. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Facilitates monitoring of inflammatory activity.

sections.title: Treatment Indications & Duration
content: General: Treatment is not always needed as spontaneous resolution occurs.
Sight-Threatening Lesion: Involving macula, papillomacular bundle, optic nerve, or major vessel.
Severe vitritis: Clear indication for therapy.
Immunocompromised Status: Always requires treatment.
Duration: Typically 4–6 weeks for antibiotics.
Healing Time: Active lesions take 4–6 months to heal completely.

content.explanation: Pyrimethamine (75-100mg load, then 25-50mg daily) + Sulfadiazine (1g QID) + Prednisolone (1mg/kg). ALWAYS add Folinic Acid (5mg 3x/week) to prevent marrow toxicity.

rows: Intravitreal
Clindamycin (1mg) + Dexamethasone (400µg). 2-3 injections 2 weeks apart. Effective as triple therapy.
Co-trimoxazole
Trimethoprim 160mg / Sulfamethoxazole 800mg BID. Low cost, better tolerated.
Azithromycin
250–500 mg daily. Shows promise in reducing recurrence rates.
Clindamycin Oral
300 mg QID. Risk of pseudomembranous colitis.
Atovaquone
750 mg 2–4 times daily. Attacks encysted bradyzoites (theoretically).

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNINGS & CONTRAINDICATIONS
content: NEVER use depot steroids (e.g., triamcinolone) intra- or periocularly (uncontrolled progression reported).
Systemic steroids should be used with extreme caution in immunocompromised patients.
Pyrimethamine: Perform weekly blood counts (risk of thrombocytopenia/leukopenia).
Sulfonamides: Risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome and renal stones.
AIDS Patients: Avoid or reduce pyrimethamine due to marrow suppression and zidovudine antagonism.
Pregnancy: Avoid pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine (fetal harm). Use Spiramycin or Intravitreal therapy.

sections.title: Recurrence & Long-term Management
content: Average Recurrences: 2.7 attacks per patient.
2-Year Risk: 12–15% recurrence rate.
5-Year Risk: Over 50% experience a further episode.
Prophylaxis Regimen: Co-trimoxazole (160/800) three times daily for 12 months.
Prophylaxis Benefit: Reduces recurrence from 22% to 3% for up to 3 years.
Neonatal Care: 1 year of antimicrobials in congenital cases may reduce future scarring.

content.explanation: Start steroids 24–48 hours AFTER starting antimicrobial therapy to ensure parasitic cover before dampening the immune response.

sections.title: Verbatim Figure Descriptions & Notes
sections.content: Fig 12.29 Life cycle includes oocysts in faeces, contaminated food/water/soil, transfusion, transplantation, and vertical transmission. Fig 12.30 identifies scars at the macula, peripapillary, upper temporal, and inferonasal periphery. Fig 12.31 illustrates 'satellite' lesions and 'headlight in the fog'. Fig 12.32 notes uncommon complications: Branch retinal artery occlusion, non-perfusion on FA, serous macular detachment, and macular neovascularization. Healing results in a sharply demarcated atrophic scar with a pigmented border (Fig 12.33). Children should undergo varicella zoster vaccination if they have not had chickenpox before starting steroids.
